items.title: GNSS NTP Graphs
items.text:
GNSS NTP Graphs draws history graphs for a GPS-disciplined NTP server, in the style of graphs1090. A small Python collector polls chrony or ntpd and gpsd, stores the readings in SQLite and writes JSON files. A static page in the browser turns those files into graphs.

It runs next to GPSNTPHomeBridge, the bridge that feeds the same server into Home Assistant, and leaves it alone. It needs Python 3.11 or newer and no pip packages.

items.title: How the pieces fit
items.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph server [Time server]
        direction TB
        sat[GNSS satellites] --> rx[GPS receiver<br/>NMEA + PPS]
        rx --> gpsd
        gpsd --> ntp[chronyd or ntpd]
        ntp --> clients[NTP clients]
    end
    subgraph collector [gnss-ntp-graphs collector]
        direction TB
        src[source: local or bridge] --> db[(SQLite<br/>samples.db)]
        db --> json[data/*.json]
        json --> page[Static page<br/>uPlot graphs]
    end
    server -. chronyc / ntpq<br/>gpsd port 2947 .-> collector
    bridge[GPSNTPHomeBridge JSON] -. HTTP .-> collector

The collector reads the server one of two ways. On the Pi with the receiver it runs chronyc or ntpq and opens a client connection to gpsd. On any other machine it fetches the JSON files the bridge already publishes. Both paths map the fields the same way, so the graphs match. Choosing a source explains the difference.

items.title: What the page shows
items.text:
Tab Graphs NTP System offset, jitter, frequency and wander, root delay and dispersion, stratum Peers Offset, delay, jitter and reach for each source, plus a table of the current peers GNSS Satellites used and visible, used satellites per constellation, average signal, DOP, sky plot Stats Percentile tables, offset histogram and Allan deviation over 24 hours and 7 days

The header carries a live status line for the server. Reading the graphs covers it field by field.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• Install on a Raspberry Pi, a Debian host or in Docker.
  • Configuration for the collector and for the page.
  • How it works for the storage tiers, timers and data files.

items.title: Development
items.text: The project uses uv. The collector itself has no dependencies; pytest, pytest-cov, ruff and Zensical sit in dependency groups.

items.title: Tests and lint
items.text:
uv run pytest --cov=gnss_ntp_graphs
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check .

The tests cover config loading and validation, the chrony, ntpd, gpsd and bridge parsers (against the captured output in tests/fixtures/), the store and rollups, the statistics, and the commit-message hook. The run fails if total coverage drops below fail_under in pyproject.toml.

The CI workflow runs the ruff checks and the tests on Python 3.11 and 3.12 for every push and pull request to main, and uploads the 3.12 coverage report to Codecov.

items.title: Running against a config
items.text:
uv run python -m gnss_ntp_graphs -c deploy/config.toml once

once polls once and writes every file, then exits. Point [paths] at a local folder first, since the defaults are under /var/lib. To watch the page, run run with the built-in server:

GNG_PATHS_DB=/tmp/gng/samples.db GNG_PATHS_WWW=/tmp/gng/www GNG_SERVER_SERVE=true \
GNG_SOURCE_BRIDGE_URL=http://192.168.1.50/ \
uv run python -m gnss_ntp_graphs run

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8080/.

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
Zensical builds this site from docs/ and zensical.toml.

uv run --group docs zensical serve        # live preview on http://127.0.0.1:8000/
uv run --group docs zensical build --strict --clean

--strict fails on broken links and on pages missing from the navigation. The docs workflow runs a spellcheck (.github/cspell.json, British English) and the strict build, then publishes to GitHub Pages when a release is published.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
Start with the service log. On an install.sh setup:

journalctl -u gnss-ntp-graphs -n 50

In Docker, use docker logs gnss-ntp-graphs.

items.title: The service does not start
items.text:
The log shows config error: followed by the key at fault. Fix the key in /etc/gnss-ntp-graphs/config.toml and restart. Validation lists what is checked.

python 3.11 or newer required from install.sh means the system Python is too old. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm and Debian 12 have 3.11.

items.title: The page says "No data yet"
items.text:
The page could not load data/current.json.

  • current.json: 404 right after install: the collector has not written its first export yet. Wait a few seconds and reload.
  • 404 that does not go away: the web server is serving a different folder. Check the alias points at /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/www/ and that [paths] www matches.
  • The page loads but nothing else does: open the browser's developer tools and check the requests to data/.

items.title: Graphs say "No data in this range"
items.text:
No samples fall in the selected range for that graph. Check the log for source warnings:

  • bridge http://.../ntpq_crv.json: ...: the bridge URL is wrong or the bridge is down. Try the URL with curl.
  • chronyc -n -c tracking: ... or ntpq -c rv: ...: the daemon command failed. Run it by hand as the gnssgraphs user.
  • gpsd 127.0.0.1:2947: ...: gpsd is not listening at that address. Check systemctl status gpsd and [source] gpsd_host.

The 30-day and 1-year ranges read the rollup tiers, which fill up as the rollup job runs every 5 minutes. A fresh install shows little there for a while.

items.title: Gaps in the graphs
items.text:
A gap means no sample in those buckets. Common causes:

  • The collector was stopped, or the host was down.
  • The daemon was unsynchronised (stratum 0 or 16). The collector keeps those readings out of the NTP graphs on purpose.
  • gpsd returned no satellites, or the bridge reported a GPS failure. The collector stores no GPS sample then.

items.title: "updated" turns amber or red
items.text: The age of current.json is past stale_warn_s or stale_bad_s. Either the collector stopped writing (check the log) or the viewing device's clock is wrong. The browser works out the age.

items.title: Offset is around ±1.6 s in Docker
items.text: When chronyd runs inside a container without permission to set the clock (chronyd -x), it measures the container host's clock against its sources but cannot correct it. Large offsets are expected in that setup. Run the collector against the real time server instead.

items.title: NMEA squashes the peer graphs
items.text: The NMEA refclock's offset is often around 100 ms, far above PPS and network servers, so the other lines sit flat at zero. Add it to [web] hide_peers, for example hide_peers = ["NMEA"], or open a shorter range and zoom with the mouse.

items.title: The Stats tab says "polled samples" after setting a log
items.text: The collector falls back to polled samples when the log path is empty, the file cannot be read, or the window holds 10 rows or fewer. Check that gnssgraphs can read the file and that the daemon writes to it (tail the file after a few minutes). Compressed rotated files are skipped.

items.title: colourblind_safe refuses my palette
items.text: With colourblind_safe = true only Paired, Dark2 and Set2 are accepted. See Theme and colours.

items.title: lighttpd alias disabled
items.text: install.sh printed lighttpd config test failed; alias disabled. Run lighttpd -tt -f /etc/lighttpd/lighttpd.conf to see the error. Another config may already define /graphs/, or mod_alias may not be loaded. Use --web builtin or --web none as a workaround.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
The collector reads one TOML file, /etc/gnss-ntp-graphs/config.toml on an install.sh setup. deploy/config.toml in the repository lists every key with its default and a comment, shown in full under Full template. Your own file only needs the keys you change.

[source]
type = "local"

[web]
title = "Garage time server"
offset_unit = "us"

Restart the service after editing: sudo systemctl restart gnss-ntp-graphs. The page settings are written to data/config.json once at start, so a browser reload alone does not pick up a change.

items.title: Where values come from
items.text:
flowchart LR
    d[Built-in defaults<br/>config.py] --> t[TOML file<br/>-c config.toml] --> e[Environment<br/>GNG_SECTION_KEY] --> v{Validate} -- ok --> run[Collector starts]
    v -- error --> stop[exit 2:<br/>config error: ...]

Each layer overrides the one before it. Any key outside [graphs] can be set from the environment as GNG_<SECTION>_<KEY> in upper case:

GNG_SOURCE_TYPE=local
GNG_SOURCE_BRIDGE_URL=http://192.168.1.50/
GNG_WEB_SECTIONS=ntp,peers          # lists are comma-separated
GNG_WEB_OFFSET_LINES=-0.01,0.01
GNG_SERVER_SERVE=true               # true/false, yes/no, on/off or 1/0

The Docker image uses this to set its paths and port.

items.title: Validation
items.text:
The collector checks the whole config before it starts and stops with a message naming the problem. A typo cannot silently fall back to a default. Some examples:

config error: [web] colour: unknown key, allowed ['colourblind_safe', 'columns', ...]
config error: [source] type: 'gps' not one of ['bridge', 'local']
config error: [web] default_range: '12h' is not in ranges ['2h', '8h', '24h', '7d', '30d', '1y']
config error: [intervals] ntp: expected int, got '60'

It refuses unknown sections and keys, values of the wrong type, choices outside the allowed set, unknown section, range or graph ids, and a palette that is not colourblind safe when colourblind_safe = true. Under systemd the message goes to the journal (journalctl -u gnss-ntp-graphs).

items.title: Sections
items.text: Section Page Controls [source] Collector Which source, bridge URL, daemon, gpsd address [intervals] Collector Poll, export, rollup and stats timers [paths] Collector Database and web root locations [retention] Collector How long each storage tier is kept [server] Collector Built-in web server [web] Web page Everything the page shows and how [graphs.<id>] Web page Fixed y-axis limits per graph [logs] Daemon logs chrony or ntpd statistics logs for the Stats tab

items.title: Full template
items.text:
Every key with its default. Copy the lines you want to change into /etc/gnss-ntp-graphs/config.toml, or into config.docker.toml for Docker.

# gnss-ntp-graphs configuration.
# After editing: sudo systemctl restart gnss-ntp-graphs
# Only the keys you change are needed; the values below are the defaults.
# Any key can also be set from the environment as GNG_<SECTION>_<KEY>,
# e.g. GNG_SOURCE_TYPE=local or GNG_WEB_SECTIONS=ntp,peers (lists comma-separated).

[source]
# "bridge": poll GPSNTPHomeBridge JSON over HTTP (standalone server, Docker)
# "local":  read chronyc/ntpq and gpsd on this machine (Pi with the GPS)
type = "bridge"
bridge_url = "http://127.0.0.1/"
# local only: "auto" | "chrony" | "ntpd"
ntp = "auto"
gpsd_host = "127.0.0.1"
gpsd_port = 2947
timeout = 10.0
# CPU temperature of the machine the collector runs on: vcgencmd measure_temp
# (Raspberry Pi), else /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp. Hosts with
# neither skip it and the temperature graphs stay hidden.
host_temp = true

[intervals]
# Seconds. The bridge refreshes NTP every 60 s and GPS every 15 s.
ntp = 60
gps = 15
host = 60
# How often the graph data is written (graphs1090 DRAW_INTERVAL). Ranges
# longer than 2h refresh once per bucket, so long ones cost little.
export = 60
rollup = 300
stats = 900

[paths]
db = "/var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/samples.db"
www = "/var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/www"
# Static web files copied into www at start; empty = bundled files
web_src = ""

[retention]
raw_days = 7.0
days_5m = 90.0
days_1h = 1095.0

[logs]
# Optional, local mode. Daemon statistics logs give finer offset data for
# the Stats page. Empty = use polled samples. See README.
chrony_tracking = ""   # e.g. "/var/log/chrony/tracking.log"
ntpd_loopstats = ""    # e.g. "/var/log/ntpstats/loopstats"

[server]
# Built-in static web server, for Docker or hosts without lighttpd/nginx
serve = false
bind = "0.0.0.0"
port = 8080

[web]
# Text in the browser tab and page heading (graphs1090 WWW_TITLE)
title = "GNSS NTP"
# Line under the heading; empty hides it (graphs1090 WWW_HEADER)
header = ""
# Link icons in the header; an empty string hides the icon
repo_url = "https://github.com/ToledoEM/gnss-ntp-graphs"
docs_url = "https://toledoem.github.io/gnss-ntp-graphs/"
# "auto" follows the viewer's system setting; "light" | "dark" force one.
# Viewers can still switch with the theme button; their choice is remembered.
theme = "auto"
# Plot colours: a ColorBrewer qualitative scheme (https://colorbrewer2.org):
# "Accent", "Dark2", "Paired", "Pastel1", "Pastel2", "Set1", "Set2", "Set3".
# Each graph takes as many colours as it has lines (at least 3), up to the
# scheme's largest set; further lines reuse the colours with dashed strokes.
palette = "Paired"
# true limits colours to the sets ColorBrewer rates colourblind safe:
# "Paired" (up to 4 colours), "Dark2" or "Set2" (3 colours). Further lines
# are dashed. Other palettes are refused when this is on.
colourblind_safe = false
# "tabs": one section at a time; "single": all sections on one page
layout = "tabs"
# Graph crossline: "hover" follows the pointer only; "last" rests on the
# newest point and fills the values under each graph
cursor = "hover"
# Sections shown, in this order: "ntp", "peers", "gps", "stats"
sections = ["ntp", "peers", "gps", "stats"]
# Graphs to hide. Ids: offset jitter freq root stratum peer-offset
# peer-delay peer-jitter peer-reach sats const ss dop sky hist adev temp
# temp-freq temp-offset
hide_graphs = []
# Range buttons, from "2h", "8h", "24h", "7d", "30d", "1y"
ranges = ["2h", "8h", "24h", "7d", "30d", "1y"]
default_range = "24h"
# Graph plot height in px (graphs1090 graph_size / lheight)
graph_height = 220
# Graphs per row: "auto" (fit width), 1, 2 or 3. Phones always get 1.
columns = "auto"
# Base font size in px (graphs1090 font_size)
font_size = 14
# Time axis zone: "local" (viewer's browser), "UTC" or an IANA name such
# as "Europe/London" (graphs1090 TZ)
timezone = "local"
# Unit for offsets, jitter, delay and dispersion: "ms" | "us"
offset_unit = "ms"
# Dashed reference lines on the offset graph, in ms, e.g. [-0.01, 0.01]
offset_lines = []
# Status colour of the current offset: green below warn, amber below bad, else red (ms)
offset_warn_ms = 1.0
offset_bad_ms = 10.0
# Status colour of the "updated" age, in seconds
stale_warn_s = 120
stale_bad_s = 300
# Most peers drawn per graph (those with the most data win)
max_peers = 16
# Peers never drawn, by remote address or name, e.g. ["NMEA"]
hide_peers = []

# Fixed y-axis limits per graph, in the graph's displayed unit
# (graphs1090 ul_* / ll_*). One table per graph id; either key may be left out.
# [graphs.offset]
# y_min = -0.05
# y_max = 0.05
#
# [graphs.dop]
# y_max = 3

items.title: Collector settings
items.text: These sections control what the collector reads, how often, and where it keeps the results. The values shown are the defaults.

items.title: source
items.text:
[source]
type = "bridge"
bridge_url = "http://127.0.0.1/"
ntp = "auto"
gpsd_host = "127.0.0.1"
gpsd_port = 2947
timeout = 10.0
host_temp = true
Key Values Meaning type bridge, local Read GPSNTPHomeBridge's JSON over HTTP, or read the daemons on this machine. See Choosing a source bridge_url URL Base URL of the bridge's web root. The collector appends ntpq_crv.json, ntpq_pn.json, gps.json and, if present, cpu_temp.json ntp auto, chrony, ntpd local only. auto uses chrony when chronyc -n -c tracking answers, otherwise ntpd gpsd_host, gpsd_port host, port local only. Where gpsd listens timeout seconds Limit for each HTTP request, command or gpsd read host_temp true, false Record the CPU temperature of the machine the collector runs on, with either source type. With bridge, the bridge's cpu_temp.json comes first. Otherwise reads vcgencmd measure_temp, else /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp. Hosts with neither skip it. See CPU temperature

With local and chrony, each NTP poll runs chronyc -n -c tracking, -c sources, -c sourcestats and chronyc -n ntpdata. With ntpd it runs ntpq -c rv and ntpq -pn. Each GPS poll connects to gpsd, sends ?WATCH, waits for the first SKY report that lists satellites and disconnects.

items.title: intervals
items.text:
[intervals]
ntp = 60
gps = 15
host = 60
export = 60
rollup = 300
stats = 900

All values are in seconds.

Key Job ntp Poll the system and peer readings gps Poll the satellite view and DOP host Read the CPU temperature export Write current.json and the range_*.json files (graphs1090 DRAW_INTERVAL) rollup Average raw samples into the 5-minute and hourly tiers, and prune old rows stats Recompute stats.json for the Stats tab

The bridge refreshes its NTP files every 60 seconds and its GPS file every 15, so polling faster than that with bridge only stores duplicates. Ranges longer than 2 hours are written once per bucket at most (every 20 minutes for 7 days, every 6 hours for 1 year), so a short export interval stays cheap. How it works shows the schedule.

items.title: paths
items.text:
[paths]
db = "/var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/samples.db"
www = "/var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/www"
web_src = ""
Key Meaning db SQLite database. The parent folder is created if missing www Web root. The collector copies the page here at start and writes data/ below it web_src Folder to copy the page from instead of the bundled one. Leave empty unless you maintain a modified page

items.title: Where data is saved
items.text:
All history is in one SQLite file, samples.db, at the db path:

Install Database Raspberry Pi or Debian (install.sh) /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/samples.db Docker /data/samples.db in the gnss-ntp-graphs volume. docker volume inspect gnss-ntp-graphs shows its folder on the host Development run Whatever GNG_PATHS_DB points to

The database runs in WAL mode, so samples.db-wal and samples.db-shm sit next to it while the collector runs. The www/ folder holds only the page and JSON files the collector rewrites, so it needs no backup.

items.title: Backing up
items.text:
A plain file copy of a running database can catch it halfway through a write. Use SQLite's backup instead, which is safe while the collector runs:

sqlite3 /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/samples.db ".backup '/home/pi/samples-$(date +%F).db'"

Without the sqlite3 tool, Python does the same:

python3 -c "import sqlite3; sqlite3.connect('/var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/samples.db').backup(sqlite3.connect('/home/pi/samples-backup.db'))"

With Docker, run the backup inside the container and copy the result out:

docker exec gnss-ntp-graphs python -c "import sqlite3; sqlite3.connect('/data/samples.db').backup(sqlite3.connect('/data/samples-backup.db'))"
docker cp gnss-ntp-graphs:/data/samples-backup.db .

The backup is a single self-contained file, with no -wal or -shm files to copy.

items.title: Restoring
items.text:
1. Stop the collector: sudo systemctl stop gnss-ntp-graphs, or docker compose stop.
  2. Replace samples.db with the backup and delete any samples.db-wal and samples.db-shm next to it.
  3. Set the file's owner to the collector's user: sudo chown gnssgraphs: /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/samples.db. In Docker the user is UID 10001.
  4. Start the collector again.

items.title: retention
items.text:
[retention]
raw_days = 7.0
days_5m = 90.0
days_1h = 1095.0
Key Tier raw_days Every polled sample. Also the window the Stats tab can look back over days_5m 5-minute averages days_1h Hourly averages. 1095 days is three years

A graph range reads the finest tier that still covers its start. With the defaults, ranges up to 7 days use raw samples, the 30-day range uses 5-minute averages and the 1-year range uses hourly averages. Keep raw_days at 7 or more, because the 7-day statistics window reads raw samples.

items.title: server
items.text:
[server]
serve = false
bind = "0.0.0.0"
port = 8080

serve = true starts the built-in static web server on bind:port. install.sh sets it when lighttpd is missing, and the Docker image always sets it. See Web server.

items.title: Daemon logs
items.text:
The Stats tab normally works from the samples the collector polls once a minute. That limits the Allan deviation to averaging times of 60 seconds and up, and history starts the day you installed the collector.

chrony and ntpd can both log every clock update to a statistics file. When the collector can read that file, the Stats tab uses it for the offset and frequency statistics, the histogram and the Allan deviation. Neither daemon writes these logs by default. The collector never changes daemon config, so turn the log on yourself and then tell the collector where it is.

This works with source.type = "local" only, since the collector reads the file from local disk.

items.title: chrony
items.text:
Add to /etc/chrony/chrony.conf:

log tracking
logdir /var/log/chrony

Restart chronyd, then set:

[logs]
chrony_tracking = "/var/log/chrony/tracking.log"

items.title: ntpd or ntpsec
items.text:
Add to /etc/ntp.conf (or /etc/ntpsec/ntp.conf):

statsdir /var/log/ntpstats/
statistics loopstats

Restart ntpd, then set:

[logs]
ntpd_loopstats = "/var/log/ntpstats/loopstats"

items.title: How the collector reads them
items.text:
flowchart TD
    s[Stats job, every 900 s] --> c{chrony_tracking set<br/>and over 10 rows in window?}
    c -- yes --> uc[use tracking.log]
    c -- no --> n{ntpd_loopstats set<br/>and over 10 rows in window?}
    n -- yes --> un[use loopstats]
    n -- no --> p[use polled samples]
  • The collector also reads rotated files next to the live one: tracking.log.1, loopstats.20261124 and so on. It skips compressed files (.gz, .xz, .bz2).
  • The sample spacing for the Allan deviation is the median gap between log rows. The Stats tab shows it as "sample spacing" next to the source name.
  • chrony logs offset as local clock minus reference. The collector flips the sign so it matches ntpq and the rest of the page.
  • The gnssgraphs user needs read access to the file.
  • Only the offset and frequency figures come from the log. Jitter, root delay, root dispersion, GNSS and peer statistics still come from polled samples.

The line under the Stats window buttons says which source is in use, for example offset source: chrony tracking.log, sample spacing 16s.

items.title: Web page settings
items.text: The [web] section decides what the page shows and how it looks. Where graphs1090's default file has a matching option, the table names it. The collector writes these values to data/config.json when it starts, so restart it after a change.

items.title: Title and links
items.text: Key Default graphs1090 Meaning title "GNSS NTP" WWW_TITLE Page heading. The browser tab shows it followed by "graphs" header "" WWW_HEADER A line under the heading. Empty hides it repo_url GitHub repository Link behind the GitHub icon. Empty hides the icon docs_url this site Link behind the book icon. Empty hides the icon

items.title: Layout
items.text:
Key Default graphs1090 Meaning layout "tabs" tabs shows one section at a time. single stacks all sections on one page, keeps the whole header on top while scrolling, and the buttons scroll to the sections sections ["ntp", "peers", "gps", "stats"] HIDE_SYSTEM Which sections appear, in this order hide_graphs [] Graph ids to leave out (list below) graph_height 220 graph_size Plot height in pixels. The stratum graph is 75% of this columns "auto" all_large Graphs per row: "auto" fits the width, or 1, 2, 3. Phones always get one font_size 14 font_size Base font size in pixels. Axis labels use 80% of it cursor "hover" hover shows values under a graph only while the pointer is over it. last marks the newest point with a dashed line and shows its values under each graph. Hovering still works, and the values go back to the newest point when the pointer leaves

Graph ids for hide_graphs and [graphs.<id>]:

Section Ids NTP offset, jitter, freq, root, stratum, temp Peers peer-offset, peer-delay, peer-jitter, peer-reach GNSS sats, const, ss, dop, sky Stats hist, adev, temp-freq, temp-offset

items.title: Time and units
items.text:
Key Default graphs1090 Meaning ranges ["2h", "8h", "24h", "7d", "30d", "1y"] Which range buttons appear. The collector only writes files for these default_range "24h" Range shown on a viewer's first visit. Must be in ranges timezone "local" TZ Time axis zone: local (the viewer's browser), UTC, or an IANA name such as Europe/London offset_unit "ms" ms or us for offset, jitter, delay and dispersion, on graphs and in tables offset_lines [] max_messages_line Dashed horizontal lines on the offset graph, in ms, for example [-0.01, 0.01]

The page remembers the last range a viewer picked, in their browser.

items.title: Status colours
items.text:
The header status line colours two values green, amber or red. See Status line.

Key Default Meaning offset_warn_ms 1.0 Offset magnitude in ms at which it turns amber offset_bad_ms 10.0 Offset magnitude in ms at which it turns red stale_warn_s 120 Age in seconds at which "updated" turns amber stale_bad_s 300 Age in seconds at which "updated" turns red

items.title: Peers
items.text:
Key Default Meaning max_peers 16 Most peers drawn per graph. Peers with the most data in the range win hide_peers [] Peers never drawn, by address or name as the peer table shows it, for example ["NMEA"]

An NMEA refclock usually has an offset far larger than the other sources (about 110 ms in the screenshots), which squashes their lines against zero. Hiding it is a common choice. The peer table and the Stats tab still list hidden peers.

items.title: Theme and colours
items.text:
Key Default graphs1090 Meaning theme "auto" colorscheme auto follows the viewer's system setting. light or dark sets the starting theme palette "Paired" Line colours, from the ColorBrewer qualitative schemes colourblind_safe false Limit colours to the sets ColorBrewer rates colourblind safe

Viewers can switch theme with the button in the header. Their browser remembers the choice, and it overrides theme.

Allowed palettes are Accent, Dark2, Paired, Pastel1, Pastel2, Set1, Set2 and Set3. Each graph takes as many colours as it has lines (at least three), up to the scheme's largest set. A graph with a single line uses the scheme's second colour, which in Paired is the darker blue. When a graph has more lines than the scheme has colours, the extra lines reuse the colours with dashed strokes.

With colourblind_safe = true only three palettes are accepted: Paired (up to 4 colours), Dark2 and Set2 (3 colours each). Lines past that count are dashed. The DOP graph below has five lines with Paired limited to four colours, so the fifth is dashed:

The sky plot draws dots, which cannot be dashed, so there the satellite numbers tell constellations apart when colours repeat.

items.title: Fixed y-axis limits
items.text:
By default every graph scales to its data. To fix an axis, add a table per graph id with y_min, y_max or both, in the unit the graph displays (graphs1090 ul_* and ll_*):

[graphs.offset]
y_min = -0.05
y_max = 0.05

[graphs.dop]
y_max = 3

With offset_unit = "us" the offset limits are in microseconds. The [graphs] tables cannot be set from the environment.

items.title: Install
items.text: The collector is plain Python 3.11 with no third-party packages. Pick where it runs and which source it reads, then follow one of the install pages.

items.title: Choosing a source
items.text:
Source Use it on Reads local The Pi with the GPS receiver chronyc -c tracking/sources/sourcestats and chronyc ntpdata, or ntpq -c rv and ntpq -pn, plus gpsd on port 2947 bridge Any other machine, or Docker ntpq_crv.json, ntpq_pn.json and gps.json from the bridge's web root

The local source only runs monitoring commands. It never changes chrony, ntpd or gpsd settings, and gpsd accepts a second client, so it runs fine next to the bridge. The bridge source sends HTTP GET requests and nothing else.

Both sources produce the same fields. Offsets, jitter and delays are in milliseconds, frequency and wander in parts per million, and the offset sign follows ntpq (source minus local clock).

With local, the daemon logs option can add finer offset data to the Stats tab. The bridge does not publish those logs, so bridge always uses polled samples.

items.title: Install methods
items.text: Method Page Typical use install.sh with systemd Raspberry Pi or Debian The time server itself, or a Debian box on the same network Docker image Docker A home server that already runs containers Your own web server Web server Serving the page from lighttpd, nginx or the built-in server

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Python 3.11 or newer. Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm ships 3.11.
  • For local: chronyc or ntpq on the path, and gpsd listening on 127.0.0.1:2947 (both configurable).
  • For bridge: network access to the bridge's web root, for example http://192.168.1.50/.

items.title: Docker
items.text: The Dockerfile builds a small image on python:3.12-slim. It runs the collector as user gnssgraphs (UID 10001), keeps its data in the /data volume and serves the page on port 8080 with the built-in web server.

items.title: Bridge source
items.text:
This is the usual setup: the container polls GPSNTPHomeBridge over HTTP.

docker build -t gnss-ntp-graphs .
docker run -d --name gnss-ntp-graphs -p 8080:8080 \
  -e GNG_SOURCE_BRIDGE_URL=http://192.168.1.50/ \
  -v gnss-ntp-graphs:/data gnss-ntp-graphs

Open http://<docker-host>:8080/.

items.title: Docker Compose with a custom config
items.text:
deploy/ has a Compose file and a config template. Keep your own copies outside the repository, so a git pull never overwrites your settings.

  1. Copy deploy/compose.yaml and deploy/config.docker.toml into a folder of your own, for example ~/gnss-ntp-graphs/.
  2. In compose.yaml, set build.context to the folder holding this repository (the one with the Dockerfile), and GNG_SOURCE_BRIDGE_URL to your bridge.
  3. Edit config.docker.toml. Only the keys you change are needed.
  4. Start it with docker compose up -d.

After a change to the TOML file, run docker compose restart. After pulling a new version of the code, run docker compose up -d --build.

The image sets source.type, source.bridge_url, paths.db, paths.www, server.serve and server.port through GNG_* environment variables, and these win over the file. Change those six under environment: in compose.yaml. Every other key goes in the TOML file.

compose.yaml:

# Docker Compose for gnss-ntp-graphs with a custom TOML config.
# Copy this file and config.docker.toml into one folder, edit the TOML, then:
#   docker compose up -d
# After editing the TOML: docker compose restart
# Set "context" to the folder holding this repository's Dockerfile.

services:
  gnss-ntp-graphs:
    build:
      context: ..
      # Local source only: include chronyc in the image
      # args:
      #   WITH_CHRONYC: "1"
    image: gnss-ntp-graphs
    container_name: gnss-ntp-graphs
    command: ["python", "-m", "gnss_ntp_graphs", "-c", "/config.toml", "run"]
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    # The image sets these through GNG_* variables, which win over the TOML
    environment:
      GNG_SOURCE_TYPE: bridge  # bridge | local
      GNG_SOURCE_BRIDGE_URL: http://192.168.1.50/
    # Local source only: read chronyd and gpsd on the Docker host.
    # Remove "ports" above when using host networking.
    # network_mode: host
    volumes:
      - gnss-ntp-graphs:/data
      - ./config.docker.toml:/config.toml:ro
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  gnss-ntp-graphs:

config.docker.toml:

# gnss-ntp-graphs configuration for Docker Compose (see compose.yaml).
# Only the keys you change are needed; anything left out keeps its default.
# Full list of keys: deploy/config.toml or the Configuration docs.
#
# The image sets source.type, source.bridge_url, paths.db, paths.www,
# server.serve and server.port through GNG_* environment variables, and the
# environment wins over this file. To change one of those, set it under
# "environment:" in compose.yaml instead (e.g. GNG_SOURCE_BRIDGE_URL).

[web]
title = "GNSS NTP"
header = ""
# "tabs" or "single"
layout = "tabs"
# "hover" or "last"
cursor = "hover"
default_range = "24h"
timezone = "local"
offset_unit = "ms"

[intervals]
ntp = 60
gps = 15
export = 60

[retention]
raw_days = 7.0
days_5m = 90.0
days_1h = 1095.0

A container has no CPU temperature sensor of its own, so the temperature graphs only appear when the bridge publishes cpu_temp.json (see Raspberry Pi).

For the local source, uncomment WITH_CHRONYC and network_mode: host, remove ports, and set GNG_SOURCE_TYPE: local.

items.title: Local source
items.text:
To read a chronyd running on the Docker host, build the image with chronyc included and give the container the host network:

docker build --build-arg WITH_CHRONYC=1 -t gnss-ntp-graphs .
docker run -d --name gnss-ntp-graphs --network host \
  -e GNG_SOURCE_TYPE=local \
  -v gnss-ntp-graphs:/data gnss-ntp-graphs

With --network host the page is on port 8080 of the host and gpsd is reachable at 127.0.0.1:2947.

items.title: Image defaults
items.text:
The image sets these environment variables. Override any of them with -e, and any other key with GNG_<SECTION>_<KEY> (see Configuration).

Variable Value GNG_SOURCE_TYPE bridge GNG_SOURCE_BRIDGE_URL http://bridge/ GNG_PATHS_DB /data/samples.db GNG_PATHS_WWW /data/www GNG_SERVER_SERVE true GNG_SERVER_PORT 8080

To use a TOML file instead, mount it and pass -c:

docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -v gnss-ntp-graphs:/data \
  -v ./config.toml:/config.toml:ro gnss-ntp-graphs \
  python -m gnss_ntp_graphs -c /config.toml run

Environment variables still win over the file.

items.title: Data and backups
items.text: The history lives in /data/samples.db inside the gnss-ntp-graphs volume. See Where data is saved for backing it up.

items.title: Health check
items.text: The image's HEALTHCHECK fetches http://127.0.0.1:8080/data/current.json every 60 seconds. docker ps shows the container as healthy once the collector has written its first export, usually within a minute of starting.

items.title: Raspberry Pi or Debian
items.text:
install.sh installs the collector as a systemd service on Debian or Raspberry Pi OS. Run it as root from a clone of the repository.

git clone https://github.com/ToledoEM/gnss-ntp-graphs
cd gnss-ntp-graphs
sudo ./install.sh                                    # local source if chronyc or ntpq is present
sudo ./install.sh --source bridge --bridge-url http://192.168.1.50/

When the script finishes it prints the address of the graphs.

items.title: Options
items.text: Option Default Effect --source bridge\|local local if chronyc or ntpq is on the path, else bridge Data source written to the new config file --bridge-url URL http://127.0.0.1/ Bridge base URL, used with --source bridge --web lighttpd\|builtin\|none lighttpd if installed, else builtin How the page is served (see below) --uninstall Removes the service, code and config, keeps the data --purge With --uninstall, also deletes /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs

items.title: What the script does
items.text: The script installs python3 if it is missing and touches nothing else. It does not change chrony, ntpd, gpsd or GPSNTPHomeBridge. A second run upgrades the code and keeps your config file.

items.title: Installed files
items.text: Path Contents /opt/gnss-ntp-graphs/gnss_ntp_graphs/ The Python package /etc/gnss-ntp-graphs/config.toml Configuration, see Configuration /etc/systemd/system/gnss-ntp-graphs.service systemd unit /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/samples.db SQLite history, see backing up /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/www/ Static page and data/*.json /etc/lighttpd/conf-available/89-gnss-ntp-graphs.conf lighttpd alias, only with --web lighttpd

items.title: The service
items.text:
The unit runs python3 -m gnss_ntp_graphs -c /etc/gnss-ntp-graphs/config.toml run as the unprivileged user gnssgraphs. It starts after the network, chrony, ntpd, ntpsec and gpsd units, and restarts 10 seconds after a failure.

systemd sandboxing keeps the collector read-only everywhere except its state directory: ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome=yes, PrivateTmp=yes, PrivateDevices=yes, NoNewPrivileges=yes and ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs. If you point [logs] at a daemon log, that file only needs to be readable by gnssgraphs.

Common commands:

sudo systemctl status gnss-ntp-graphs
sudo systemctl restart gnss-ntp-graphs     # after editing config.toml
journalctl -u gnss-ntp-graphs -f           # follow the log

items.title: CPU temperature
items.text:
The collector records the CPU temperature every [intervals] host seconds (60 by default) and graphs it against the frequency correction. Set [source] host_temp = false to turn it off.

Where the reading comes from depends on where the collector runs.

Collector runs on Temperature of Read from The GPS Pi (local or bridge) The GPS Pi /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp under the service, vcgencmd measure_temp when run by hand Another machine or Docker (bridge) The GPS Pi, if the bridge publishes cpu_temp.json <bridge_url>/cpu_temp.json Another machine, bridge without cpu_temp.json That machine, if it has a sensor Its own thermal zone

The service runs with PrivateDevices=yes, which hides /dev/vchiq, so vcgencmd cannot run inside it. The kernel thermal zone is the same sensor and stays readable. Check both by hand on the Pi:

vcgencmd measure_temp                          # temp=48.3'C
cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp      # 48312 (millidegrees)

items.title: Publishing the temperature from the bridge
items.text:
GPSNTPHomeBridge does not publish a temperature file itself. To get the GPS Pi's temperature into a collector on another machine, add a timer on the Pi that writes cpu_temp.json into the bridge's web root (/var/www/html by default):

{"timestamp": 1795535340, "cpu_temp": 48.3}

timestamp is Unix seconds or an ISO 8601 string. The collector ignores a file older than 5 minutes, so a stopped timer shows as a gap rather than a flat line.

/usr/local/bin/cpu-temp-json:

#!/bin/sh
# Write the CPU temperature as cpu_temp.json for gnss-ntp-graphs
out=/var/www/html/cpu_temp.json
milli=$(cat /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp) || exit 1
printf '{"timestamp": %s, "cpu_temp": %s.%03d}\n' "$(date +%s)" "$((milli / 1000))" "$((milli % 1000))" > "$out.tmp"
mv "$out.tmp" "$out"

Make it executable and run it every minute from root's crontab:

sudo chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/cpu-temp-json
(sudo crontab -l 2>/dev/null; echo '* * * * * /usr/local/bin/cpu-temp-json') | sudo crontab -

Check it with curl http://<bridge>/cpu_temp.json. The collector picks the file up on its next poll; no restart is needed.

items.title: Uninstall
items.text:
sudo ./install.sh --uninstall              # keeps /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs
sudo ./install.sh --uninstall --purge      # deletes the collected history too

Uninstall stops and removes the service, the lighttpd alias, /opt/gnss-ntp-graphs and /etc/gnss-ntp-graphs.

items.title: Web server
items.text: The collector writes a static site to /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/www: index.html, the scripts and styles, and a data/ folder of JSON files it rewrites every minute. Any web server that can serve a folder will do. The one special rule: send data/ with Cache-Control: no-cache, so browsers always fetch fresh numbers.

items.title: lighttpd
items.text:
GPSNTPHomeBridge's full install already runs lighttpd, and install.sh --web lighttpd adds an alias next to the bridge's files. The graphs then appear at http://<host>/graphs/. The snippet it installs is deploy/lighttpd-gnss-ntp-graphs.conf:

server.modules += ( "mod_setenv" )

alias.url += ( "/graphs/" => "/var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/www/" )

$HTTP["url"] =~ "^/graphs/data/" {
    setenv.add-response-header = ( "Cache-Control" => "no-cache" )
}

To add it by hand:

sudo cp deploy/lighttpd-gnss-ntp-graphs.conf /etc/lighttpd/conf-available/89-gnss-ntp-graphs.conf
sudo lighty-enable-mod gnss-ntp-graphs
sudo systemctl reload lighttpd

The installer runs lighttpd -tt before reloading. If the test fails it disables the alias again and prints lighttpd config test failed; alias disabled.

items.title: nginx
items.text:
Put the contents of deploy/nginx-gnss-ntp-graphs.conf inside an existing server { } block:

location /graphs/ {
    alias /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/www/;
    index index.html;
}
location /graphs/data/ {
    alias /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/www/data/;
    add_header Cache-Control no-cache;
}

Install the collector with --web none so it does not try to set up lighttpd.

items.title: Built-in server
items.text:
With no web server on the host, the collector serves the folder itself. install.sh turns this on when lighttpd is missing, and the Docker image always uses it.

[server]
serve = true
bind = "0.0.0.0"
port = 8080

It is Python's threaded http.server, sends no-cache on data/, and logs requests only at debug level (-v). It has no TLS or authentication, so keep it on your local network.

items.title: Under a different path
items.text: The page loads everything with relative URLs, so it works at the site root, under /graphs/ or under any other prefix without changes.

items.title: Reading the graphs
items.text: The page has a header with a live status line, a row of section tabs and range buttons, and the graphs of the chosen section.

items.title: Status line
items.text:
The status line shows the newest readings from data/current.json. It does not follow the range buttons.

Field Meaning refid Reference the server is locked to. PPS or GPS for a receiver, an IP address when it follows another server stratum 1 when locked to the receiver. Higher means it follows a network server. 16 or 0 means not synchronised offset System clock offset from its reference, in the offset unit sync peer The peer marked * in the peer table, or none leap Leap second status: Normal, Insert second, Delete second or Not synchronised sats Satellites used / visible in the latest gpsd SKY report updated Seconds since the collector last wrote current.json

Two fields change colour:

Field Green Amber Red offset below offset_warn_ms (1 ms) below offset_bad_ms (10 ms) at or above offset_bad_ms updated up to stale_warn_s (120 s) up to stale_bad_s (300 s) over stale_bad_s

The limits are configurable. A red "updated" means the collector has stopped writing, or the browser cannot reach the files. The page works out the age from the viewer's own clock, so a badly set clock on the viewing device also shows up here.

If the page cannot load current.json at all, the status line shows No data yet: followed by the error, for example current.json: 404 before the first export.

items.title: Tabs and ranges
items.text:
The tabs switch between the NTP, Peers, GNSS and Stats sections. The address bar follows the tab (#ntp, #peers, #gps, #stats), so you can bookmark a section. With layout = "single" all sections sit on one page and the buttons scroll to them.

The range buttons pick the time span: 2 hours, 8 hours, 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or 1 year. Each range averages samples into buckets:

Range Bucket Storage tier read 2h 30 s raw 8h 1 min raw 24h 3 min raw 7d 20 min raw 30d 1 h 5-minute averages 1y 6 h hourly averages

Longer ranges therefore smooth out short spikes. Zoom into a shorter range to see them. A bucket with no samples is left empty, so outages show as gaps in the line. The Stats tab has its own 24h and 7d buttons and hides the range buttons.

items.title: Using a graph
items.text:
• Hover over a graph to read exact values in the legend below it.
  • Drag across a graph to zoom the time axis. Double-click to zoom back out.
  • Click a legend entry to hide or show that line.
  • The page reloads its data every 60 seconds. Resizing the window redraws the graphs.

The theme button cycles through auto, light and dark. The browser remembers the choice, along with the last tab and range.

items.title: Footer
items.text: The footer shows the collector version, the source type (bridge or local) and when the shown data was written.

items.title: GNSS
items.text:
The GNSS tab shows the receiver's view of the sky, from gpsd's SKY reports. With the bridge source the same data arrives through the bridge's gps.json. The collector polls it every 15 seconds.

A timing receiver needs fewer satellites than a navigation receiver, especially once its position is fixed, but more satellites with good geometry make the PPS edge steadier and keep the server on stratum 1 through partial sky blockage.

items.title: Satellites used and visible
items.text:
visible counts every satellite in the report. used counts those the receiver includes in its solution. Values are averaged per bucket, so they can be fractional.

Some distance between the two lines is normal: low satellites and weak signals are tracked but left out. A drop in used at the same time each day often points to a building or tree blocking part of the sky. If the receiver loses the sky or gpsd stops answering, the collector stores no GPS sample and the graph shows a gap.

items.title: Used by constellation
items.text:
Satellites in use per system: gps, galileo, glonass, beidou, qzss, sbas and navic. Only constellations seen during the range get a line. The constellation comes from gpsd's gnssid field, and each constellation keeps its colour across this graph and the sky plot.

Which systems appear depends on the receiver model and its configuration. A receiver set to GPS only shows one line.

items.title: Average signal
items.text: The mean signal strength (carrier-to-noise density, ss in gpsd) of the satellites in use, in dB-Hz. With a roof antenna, values in the 30s and 40s are typical. Values in the 20s suggest a poor antenna position, a long or damaged cable, or interference. A daily dip that matches the satellite count usually means part of the sky is blocked.

items.title: Dilution of precision
items.text:
DOP values describe how the geometry of the satellites in use multiplies measurement error. Lower is better. Values under 1 are excellent and under 2 are good.

Line Covers hdop Horizontal position vdop Vertical position pdop 3D position tdop Time gdop Position and time together

For a time server TDOP matters most. It rises when few satellites are in use or they cluster in one part of the sky.

items.title: Sky now
items.text:
A polar plot of the latest SKY report. It always shows the current view and ignores the range buttons.

  • North is up and east is right. The centre is straight overhead (90° elevation). The rings mark 60°, 30° and the horizon.
  • Each circle is a satellite, labelled with its PRN number and coloured by constellation.
  • A filled circle is in use. A hollow circle is visible but not used.
  • Circle size follows signal strength, from smallest at 10 dB-Hz or below to largest at 50 dB-Hz.
  • Satellites below the horizon or without a position are left out.

Hollow circles near the outer ring are expected: receivers usually skip satellites below an elevation mask. A cluster of hollow or small circles in one direction shows where the antenna's view is blocked. If the plot reads "no satellite data", gpsd returned no satellites in its last report.

items.title: NTP
items.text:
The NTP tab shows how well the server's own clock follows its reference. All five graphs come from the system variables: chronyc tracking for chrony, ntpq -c rv for ntpd.

flowchart LR
    gnss[GNSS satellites] --> rx[Receiver]
    rx -- PPS pulse --> d[chronyd / ntpd]
    rx -- NMEA time --> d
    net[Network NTP servers] -.-> d
    d -- disciplines --> clk[System clock]
    clk --> cl[NTP clients]

The receiver's pulse-per-second (PPS) output marks the start of each second precisely, and the NMEA sentences say which second it is. The daemon steers the system clock towards that reference. These graphs show how far off the clock is, how noisy the measurement is, and how hard the daemon has to steer.

items.title: Offset
items.text:
The difference between the system clock and the reference at each update. The sign follows ntpq: positive means the reference is ahead of the local clock.

Unit ms or µs (offset_unit) chrony Last offset from tracking, sign flipped to match ntpq ntpd offset from ntpq -c rv

A PPS-locked server usually stays within tens of microseconds of zero, as in the screenshot (±0.02 ms). A slow wave over the day often follows room temperature. Steps or spikes come from the reference changing, the receiver losing lock, or the daemon falling back to network servers. The offset_lines setting draws dashed reference lines, for example at your accuracy target.

items.title: Jitter
items.text:
Two measures of short-term noise in the offset.

Line chrony ntpd sys_jitter RMS offset from tracking sys_jitter: combined jitter of the selected sources clk_jitter Standard deviation of the sync source from sourcestats clk_jitter: jitter of the clock discipline

Flat, low jitter means a clean PPS signal. A jump in jitter with a steady offset usually means a noisier reference, such as a switch from PPS to NMEA or to a network server.

items.title: Frequency and wander
items.text:
frequency (left axis) is the correction in parts per million the daemon applies to the local oscillator. A crystal is never exactly on frequency, so a steady value of a few ppm is normal. The correction moves with temperature, which shows as a daily wave or as a step when a fan or heater switches on.

wander (right axis) is the daemon's estimate of how unstable that frequency is. ntpd reports it as clk_wander. For chrony the collector uses the skew value from tracking, as the bridge does. Lower is steadier.

Unit ppm chrony frequency and skew from tracking ntpd frequency and clk_wander from ntpq -c rv

items.title: Root delay and dispersion
items.text:
root delay is the total round-trip network delay from this server back to the stratum 0 reference. For a server locked to its own receiver it is zero, as in the screenshot. It rises when the server follows a network source.

root dispersion is the daemon's running estimate of the maximum error relative to the reference. It grows between updates and resets as new samples arrive. Together they bound how wrong the clock can be: the error stays within root dispersion plus half the root delay.

Unit ms or µs (offset_unit) chrony Root delay, Root dispersion from tracking ntpd rootdelay, rootdisp from ntpq -c rv

items.title: Stratum
items.text:
The server's distance from the reference. Stratum 1 means it takes time directly from the receiver. Stratum 2 or higher means it has fallen back to a network server, which usually lines up with a GNSS outage on the GNSS tab.

When the daemon reports stratum 0 or 16 it is not synchronised, and its other values are placeholders (chrony reports a root delay of 1 s, for example). The collector keeps those readings out of every NTP graph, so they appear as a gap, while the status line still shows the current state.

items.title: CPU temperature
items.text:
CPU temperature (°C, left axis) drawn against the frequency correction (ppm, right axis). With bridge, it comes from the bridge's cpu_temp.json when the bridge publishes one. Otherwise it is the temperature of the machine the collector runs on: vcgencmd measure_temp on a Raspberry Pi, /sys/class/thermal/thermal_zone0/temp on other Linux hosts. With no reading at all, the graph stays hidden. CPU temperature explains each setup. Turn it off with [source] host_temp = false.

The crystal that sets the system clock sits next to the CPU, so its frequency follows CPU temperature. When the two lines rise and fall together, the frequency correction is thermal drift. A load spike, a fan switching on or sunlight on the case shows in both. The Stats tab puts a number on the relationship.

Unit °C and ppm Source Bridge cpu_temp.json, else vcgencmd measure_temp, else the kernel thermal zone

items.title: Peers
items.text:
The Peers tab shows each time source the daemon polls: the PPS and NMEA refclocks and any network servers. The data comes from chronyc sources and sourcestats for chrony, or ntpq -pn for ntpd.

Each graph has one line per peer, up to max_peers (16). When there are more, the peers with the most data in the range are drawn. hide_peers removes peers from the graphs by name. See Peers settings.

items.title: Peer offset
items.text:
The offset of each source measured against the local clock, in ms or µs. The selected source sits near zero because the daemon steers the clock to it. The others show how far they disagree with it.

An NMEA refclock usually shows a large, steady offset (about 110 ms in the screenshot). The serial sentence arrives well after the second it describes, which is why the daemon relies on PPS for the edge and NMEA only to number the seconds. Add the NMEA name to hide_peers if it flattens the other lines.

items.title: Peer delay
items.text: Round-trip network delay to each source. Refclocks have no network path and read zero. For network servers, rising delay usually means congestion on the way, and it makes their offsets less trustworthy.

items.title: Peer jitter
items.text: Short-term noise of each source's offset. ntpd reports it directly. For chrony the collector uses the standard deviation from sourcestats. A good PPS source has jitter in the low microseconds. NMEA jitter is usually milliseconds.

items.title: Peer reach
items.text:
The reach register records whether each of the last eight polls got an answer, one bit per poll. The graph shows it as a decimal number:

Value Octal (peer table) Meaning 255 377 All of the last 8 polls answered 254 376 The newest poll failed 127 177 The 8th poll back failed, the rest answered 0 0 No answer in the last 8 polls

On longer ranges the graph averages reach over each bucket, so a brief loss shows as a dip to a value such as 240 instead of a clean bit pattern. A line that stays at 255 is healthy.

items.title: Peers now
items.text:
The table under the graphs lists the peers from the latest poll, in the layout of ntpq -p.

Column Meaning remote Tally code, then the source address or refclock name refid The source's own reference: .PPS. or .GPS. for a refclock, an address for a network server st Stratum of the source. Refclocks show 0 t Type: u unicast server, l local refclock, s symmetric peer. ntpd can also show b broadcast, m multicast and p pool poll Poll interval in seconds reach Reach register in octal, 377 when the last 8 polls all answered delay, offset, jitter Latest values, in the offset unit

Tally codes say what the daemon thinks of each source:

Code ntpd chrony * System peer, the clock follows it Selected source + Candidate, included in the combined solution Combined with the selected source - Outlier, discarded by the clustering step Not combined, or too variable (~) x Falseticker, disagrees with the majority Falseticker # Selected but not used, over the source limit o PPS peer . Excess, dropped from the candidate list blank Rejected or unreachable Not usable

The screenshot shows a typical GPS server: PPS is the system peer, NMEA is a falseticker because its offset is far from the others, and the network server is an outlier kept as a fallback.

items.title: Stats
items.text: The Stats tab summarises the server's performance over the last 24 hours or 7 days, in the style of NTPsec's ntpviz. The collector recomputes it every 15 minutes ([intervals] stats).

items.title: Window and source
items.text:
The 24h and 7d buttons pick the window. The range buttons are hidden on this tab.

The line next to them says where the offset figures come from and how far apart the samples are:

Source shown Meaning polled samples The collector's own polls, one per [intervals] ntp (60 s) chrony tracking.log chrony's statistics log, see Daemon logs ntpd loopstats ntpd's statistics log

"Sample spacing" is the median gap between samples. It is the shortest averaging time on the Allan deviation graph. The time at the end says when the collector last computed the page.

items.title: Offset histogram
items.text:
How often each offset value occurred during the window, in 50 bins. The bins span the central 98% of samples, from the 1st to the 99th percentile. Samples outside that span are added to the end bins, so a tall bar at either edge holds the outliers from that side.

A narrow, symmetric peak centred on zero is what you want. A peak away from zero means a constant bias, for example an uncorrected cable or receiver delay. Two peaks usually mean the server switched between references during the window.

items.title: Allan deviation
items.text:
The Allan deviation (ADEV) measures frequency stability against averaging time tau. Both axes are logarithmic. Tau is in seconds, and ADEV is a fraction (1e-9 means one part per billion).

The collector computes the overlapping Allan deviation from the offset samples, after placing them on a regular grid at the sample spacing. It picks averaging factors about ten per decade, up to 30 points, and skips any sample triple that crosses a gap.

Read it from left to right. The curve normally falls as tau grows, because averaging cancels short-term noise. Where it flattens or turns upward, a slower effect such as temperature drift takes over. With polled samples the curve starts at 60 s, so a daemon log with finer spacing shows more of the short-term end.

items.title: Frequency and offset vs CPU temperature
items.text:
One point per bucket (5 minutes in the 24h window, 30 minutes in 7d) with the CPU temperature on the x axis and the average frequency correction or offset on the y axis. The dashed line is the least-squares fit. The caption gives:

slope Change per °C: ppm/°C for frequency, ms/°C (or µs/°C) for offset r Pearson correlation, from -1 to 1 n Number of buckets with both values

For frequency, an r close to 1 or -1 means temperature explains most of the correction, and the slope is the crystal's temperature coefficient at this operating point. Typical crystals sit around 0.1 to 1 ppm/°C. An r near 0 means something else drives the frequency, or the temperature hardly moved in the window. Offset is normally centred on zero whatever the temperature, because the daemon steers it there. A clear slope in the offset plot means the daemon lags behind fast temperature changes; a longer poll interval or a steadier case temperature helps.

Both graphs are hidden on hosts that record no CPU temperature.

items.title: System and GNSS table
items.text:
One row per quantity, with these columns:

Column Meaning n Number of samples in the window mean Arithmetic mean stddev Sample standard deviation p1, p5, p50, p95, p99 Percentiles, with linear interpolation between samples. p50 is the median range90 p95 minus p5: the span holding the central 90% of samples range98 p99 minus p1: the span holding the central 98%

Rows:

Row Source offset System offset (from the daemon log if configured) sys jitter System jitter frequency ppm Frequency correction (from the daemon log if configured) root delay, root disp Root delay and dispersion CPU temp °C CPU temperature of the collector's host sats used Satellites in use avg SNR dB-Hz Average signal of satellites in use TDOP, HDOP Time and horizontal dilution of precision

range90 and range98 are the most useful single numbers for comparing periods. Unlike the standard deviation, a handful of outliers barely moves them.

GNSS rows have more samples than system rows because the collector polls GPS every 15 seconds instead of every 60.

items.title: Peers table
items.text:
Column Meaning remote Peer address or name. Peers in hide_peers are still listed here n Number of polls in the window offset p50 Median offset offset 90% range p95 minus p5 of the offset delay p50, jitter p50 Median delay and jitter reach 377 % Share of polls where all of the last 8 polls had answered (reach 377 octal)

A reach 377 share below 100% on a network server means lost packets. On a refclock it means the receiver or gpsd dropped out.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
The collector is one Python process with no third-party dependencies. It polls a source, stores samples in SQLite and writes JSON files. The browser does all the drawing, with a bundled copy of uPlot, so the server only serves small static files.

flowchart LR
    subgraph sources [Sources]
        L[LocalSource<br/>chronyc / ntpq / gpsd]
        B[BridgeSource<br/>HTTP GET JSON]
    end
    L --> S
    B --> S
    S[Normalised samples<br/>system, peers, gps] --> DB[(SQLite store)]
    DB --> E[Exporter]
    E --> C[data/current.json]
    E --> R[data/range_*.json]
    E --> T[data/stats.json]
    E --> G[data/config.json]
    C --> P[index.html + app.js]
    R --> P
    T --> P
    G --> P
Module Job sources/local.py Runs chronyc or ntpq and reads gpsd, then converts the output to the bridge's JSON shape sources/bridge.py Fetches ntpq_crv.json, ntpq_pn.json and gps.json from the bridge sources/base.py Turns either shape into SystemSample, PeerSample and GpsSample records store.py SQLite tables, rollup tiers and range queries export.py Writes the JSON files the page reads stats.py Percentiles, histogram and Allan deviation logs.py Reads chrony tracking.log and ntpd loopstats collector.py Timer loop and the built-in web server config.py Defaults, TOML and environment loading, validation

items.title: One field mapping
items.text:
The local source converts chrony output into the same JSON shape that GPSNTPHomeBridge publishes, using the same rules as the bridge's ntp_service_chronyd.sh. Both sources then go through one parser. That is why graphs from a Pi running local and a Docker host running bridge match.

Field chrony (chronyc -c) ntpd (ntpq) offset tracking last offset, negated, in ms rv offset sys_jitter tracking RMS offset, in ms rv sys_jitter clk_jitter sourcestats std dev of the sync source, in ms rv clk_jitter frequency tracking frequency, ppm rv frequency wander tracking skew, ppm rv clk_wander rootdelay, rootdisp tracking, in ms rv rootdelay, rootdisp stratum, refid, leap tracking rv peers sources, sourcestats and ntpdata -pn

Two kinds of reading are filtered on the way in:

  • The bridge turns a gpsd failure into a record with zero satellites and no timestamp. The collector treats that as missing data, not as "0 satellites".
  • A system reading with stratum 0 or 16 (unsynchronised) carries placeholder values. It updates the status line but is kept out of the graphs.

items.title: Timers
items.text:
The main loop runs five jobs, each on its own interval from [intervals]. A job that raises an error is logged and the others carry on.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Collector
    participant Src as Source
    participant DB as SQLite
    participant Web as www/data
    Note over C: start: copy page, write config.json
    loop every 15 s (gps)
        C->>Src: gps()
        Src-->>DB: add_gps
    end
    loop every 60 s (ntp)
        C->>Src: system(), peers()
        Src-->>DB: add_system, add_peers
    end
    loop every 60 s (export)
        C->>Web: current.json
        C->>Web: range_*.json whose bucket has passed
    end
    loop every 300 s (rollup)
        C->>DB: average into 5 min and 1 h tiers, prune
    end
    loop every 900 s (stats)
        C->>Web: stats.json
    end

All jobs run once straight after start, so the page has data within seconds.

items.title: Storage tiers
items.text:
Every table exists three times: raw samples, 5-minute averages and hourly averages.

flowchart LR
    raw[raw samples<br/>kept 7 days] -- average per 5 min --> m5[5-minute tier<br/>kept 90 days]
    m5 -- average per hour --> h1[hourly tier<br/>kept 3 years]

The rollup job rebuilds only the buckets touched since its last run, then deletes rows older than each tier's retention. Text fields such as refid take the maximum value within a bucket.

When the page asks for a range, the store picks the finest tier whose retention covers the range start, then averages it into the range's bucket size. Buckets with no samples are written as null, which the graph draws as a gap.

Range Bucket Tier (defaults) Points 2h 30 s raw 240 8h 60 s raw 480 24h 180 s raw 480 7d 20 min raw 504 30d 1 h 5-minute 720 1y 6 h hourly 1460

The exporter rewrites each range file only after its bucket length has passed, so the 1-year file changes four times a day.

The database runs in SQLite WAL mode. Each sample is written as one row per timestamp, and the peers tables have one row per peer and timestamp.

items.title: The page
items.text: index.html and app.js are static. On load the page reads data/config.json, then fetches current.json and the range file for the selected tab every 60 seconds. It draws only the visible section, so hidden tabs are not drawn. Requests add a cache-busting query string, and the web server sends no-cache for data/.

items.title: Command line
items.text:
python -m gnss_ntp_graphs [-c CONFIG] [-v] [--version] [run|once]

When installed as a package the same command is available as gnss-ntp-graphs.

Argument Meaning -c, --config FILE TOML config file. Without it the collector uses the built-in defaults plus any GNG_* environment variables -v, --verbose Debug logging, including the built-in web server's requests --version Print the version and exit run Default. Copy the page into the web root, then poll and export until stopped once One poll of NTP and GPS, a rollup, and a full export of every file, then exit

run stops cleanly on SIGTERM or SIGINT (Ctrl+C).

once is handy for checking a config or a source without starting the service:

python3 -m gnss_ntp_graphs -c /etc/gnss-ntp-graphs/config.toml -v once
ls /var/lib/gnss-ntp-graphs/www/data/

Run it as the gnssgraphs user (sudo -u gnssgraphs ...) on an installed system, so the files it creates keep the right owner.

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
Code Meaning 0 Normal exit 2 Config error, or bad arguments. The message names the key, for example config error: [web] theme: 'blue' not one of ['auto', 'dark', 'light']

Problems reading a source are not fatal. The collector logs a warning such as bridge http://192.168.1.50/gps.json: <error> or gpsd 127.0.0.1:2947: <error>, skips that sample and tries again on the next interval.

items.title: Data files
items.text:
The collector writes four kinds of JSON file to www/data/. They are plain files, so you can fetch them with curl or feed them into other tools. The collector writes each file to a temporary name first and renames it into place, so a reader never sees a half-written file.

Units match the rest of the page: offsets, jitter, delay and dispersion in ms, frequency and wander in ppm, signal in dB-Hz.

items.title: config.json
items.text:
Written once at start. It holds the resolved [web] settings, the [graphs] y-axis limits and the colours of the chosen palette.

{
  "web": {"title": "GNSS NTP", "theme": "auto", "ranges": ["2h", "8h", "24h", "7d", "30d", "1y"], "...": "..."},
  "graphs": {"offset": {"y_min": -0.05, "y_max": 0.05}},
  "palette": {"classes": {"3": ["#a6cee3", "#1f78b4", "#b2df8a"], "...": []}, "safe": 4}
}

palette.safe is the largest colour count ColorBrewer rates colourblind safe for the scheme (0 if none).

items.title: current.json
items.text:
Written every [intervals] export seconds. The status line, the peer table and the sky plot read it.

  "version": "0.1.0",
  "source": "bridge",
  "constellations": ["gps", "galileo", "glonass", "beidou", "qzss", "sbas", "navic"],
  "system": {"ts": 1795535355, "offset": -0.004259, "sys_jitter": 0.004362, "clk_jitter": 0.002861,
             "frequency": -4.3421, "wander": 0.005, "rootdelay": 0.0, "rootdisp": 0.013174,

             "type": "l", "poll": 16.0, "reach": 255, "delay": 0.0, "offset": -0.002433, "jitter": 0.002}],
  "gps": {"ts": 1795535341, "total": 16, "used": 13, "avg_ss": 40.22,
          "visible_by": {"gps": 6, "galileo": 3, "glonass": 3, "beidou": 2, "qzss": 1, "sbas": 1, "navic": 0},

items.title: range_<name>.json
items.text:
One file per entry in [web] ranges: range_2h.json, range_8h.json, range_24h.json, range_7d.json, range_30d.json, range_1y.json.

{
  "name": "24h", "start": 1795874414, "end": 1795960980, "step": 180, "generated": 1795960814,
  "system": {"t": [1795874400, 1795874580], "offset": [0.0012, null], "sys_jitter": [], "...": []},
  "gps": {"t": [], "total": [], "used": [], "avg_ss": [], "vis_gps": [], "used_gps": [], "hdop": [], "...": []},
  "host": {"t": [1795874400, 1795874580], "cpu_temp": [48.1, 48.3]},
  "peers": {"PPS(0)": {"t": [], "offset": [], "delay": [], "jitter": [], "reach": []}}
}

Every array lines up with its t array, one value per bucket of step seconds. A bucket without samples holds null.

Block Series system offset, sys_jitter, clk_jitter, frequency, wander, rootdelay, rootdisp, stratum gps total, used, avg_ss, vis_<constellation>, used_<constellation>, hdop, vdop, pdop, gdop, tdop host cpu_temp (°C), on the same buckets as system peers.<remote> offset, delay, jitter, reach

peers holds at most max_peers entries and leaves out hide_peers.

items.title: stats.json
items.text:
Written every [intervals] stats seconds.

{
  "generated": 1795960814,
  "windows": {
    "24h": {
      "origin": "polled", "tau0": 60,
      "offset": {"n": 1324, "min": -0.02, "max": 0.02, "mean": 0.0001, "stddev": 0.0056,
                 "p1": -0.0143, "p5": -0.0099, "p50": 0.0003, "p95": 0.0091, "p99": 0.0121,
                 "range90": 0.019, "range98": 0.0263},
      "offset_hist": {"x": [], "count": [], "width": 0.0005},
      "frequency": {}, "sys_jitter": {}, "rootdelay": {}, "rootdisp": {},
      "adev": {"tau": [60, 120], "adev": [3.1e-8, 2.2e-8]},
      "cpu_temp": {},
      "thermal": {"step": 300, "temp": [48.1], "frequency": [-4.31], "offset": [0.0002],
                  "fit_frequency": {"slope": 0.021, "intercept": -5.32, "r": 0.93, "n": 288},
                  "fit_offset": {"slope": 0.0001, "intercept": -0.004, "r": 0.12, "n": 288}},
      "gps": {"used": {}, "avg_ss": {}, "tdop": {}, "hdop": {}},
      "peers": {"192.168.1.10": {"offset": {}, "delay": {}, "jitter": {}, "reach_full_pct": 93.9}}
    },
    "7d": {}
  }
}

origin is polled, chrony_tracking or ntpd_loopstats. tau0 is the sample spacing in seconds. adev.tau is in seconds and adev.adev is a dimensionless fraction. Each summary object has the same keys as offset. A summary is null when the window has no samples.

thermal pairs the CPU temperature with the average frequency (ppm) and offset (ms) per bucket of step seconds (300 for 24h, 1800 for 7d). The three arrays line up. fit_* is the least-squares line y = slope * temp + intercept with Pearson r and pair count n, or null with fewer than 3 pairs. thermal is null when the window has no temperature readings.
